en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
How many eyes, how many skulls, how many skins of leopards and elephants,
how many crows, how many serpents, and how many fragments of the moon are there?
Moreover, O Mother of the three worlds, how many are you within the belly of the flood of your waters?
It arises by taking up each individual member of the multitude of sentient beings that are immersed therein. || 1 ||
O Goddess, for those who dwell upon the courtyard of your sandy bank— free from pride, possessed of wisdom, and whose bodies are purified by a meager diet— a hut of grass leads to their highest good;
not so elsewhere on this earth, even if protected by hundreds of lords of the realm.
The palace, elevated like the coils of the lord of serpents, was attained by throngs of beautiful women.

O Goddess Gaṅgā, what is the use of resorting to those hundreds of hardships at various holy fords, or of performing sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma which are devoid of purpose and turned away from the Lord, and which bestow only contempt? If one may dwell in a hut on your bank without exertion, you produce a fortune more delightful than the abodes of the gods, Keśava, Vāsava, and the rest.
Those who, having reached the banks of the Gaṅgā and leaning against the cool rocks of the Golden Mountain (Meru), heard the roar of the waves out of restless curiosity,
now sit upon the lion-thrones of the rocky peaks of the mountain of the gods (Mount Meru) and listen [to that same roar].
The steady sound of the anklets of the beautiful women, perfected by their pure mastery of the Saṅgītāgama.
Go far away with your beard; we shall not even look upon your face, O wretched Pārāka! Go along with those other miserable ones who bestow heaven.
For the dust raised by the suddenly blowing gentle breeze has now reached the surface of your cheeks.
A drop of Ganges water is considered worthy for one who has abandoned attachment to courtesans. || 5 ||
She brings about union with Viṣṇu; she wanders through the forest of Śiva’s matted locks;
she wards off the need for other penances; she expands the abundance of merit with her drops of water;
she cleaves the mountain caves; and she delivers those who are submerged in her own waters.
Victorious is the Ganges, who dwells in heaven, who captivates the mind, and who is the highest good.

O Mother, daughter of King Jahnu, who else could rescue that man— talkative, crippled, wicked, full of impurity, agitated by lust, distracted, outcaste, fickle, having swallowed poison, and defiled by every fault— who has fallen into the Kumbhīpāka hell, were it not for a single drop of your water drawn from the hand of Antaka?
When the body— distressed by the fire of the digestive heat that clings and does not cling, choked with phlegm in the throat, and fouled by the gurgling sound— is closing its eyes in death,
even a man who meditates upon her attains liberation, though she is exceedingly fragile and difficult to bear.
The Jahnavi dwells within the minds of those who bathe [in her], removing the torment of saṃsāra.
Thus ends the Gaṅgāṣṭaka Stotra composed by the illustrious Kālidāsa.

Salutations to you, O Gaṅgā! By contact with your body, elephants, horses, deer, and monkeys become the limbs of the bodiless Lord (Anaṅga); they become possessed of Śiva’s body, their own bodies embraced by the Lord of Serpents (Bhujaṅgādhipa). || 1 ||
Omniscient homage to you, O Daughter of Jahnu! I do not consider the natural moon-mark and other such signs to be sufficient for the Lord of the World;
therefore, I bow to you, the virtuous one whose name is sung by Vasiṣṭha and others, O you of pure waters.
Upon your immersion, whether he be a virtuous man or a wicked one, he becomes equal to the gods in their celestial chariots through equal honors;
thus he arrives in that world of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva), where the realms of the Guardians of the Quarters are confined within the city gates.
Even the thunderbolt-bearing Indra, whose mind has become steady through the hope of embracing Rambhā,
desires to spend his days dwelling in a cottage within the grove of trees on your shore.
Victorious are your waves, which, slightly slipping from the boundary of the Lord of the Three Worlds’ mass of matted hair,
were struck by Bhavānī’s hand due to her intense anger at his transgression of her domain.

May the mind sport in the waves of the daughter of Jahnu, where the thick vermilion dye— splashing and falling from the temples of the rutting Airāvata as he plunges through the lotuses— is occasionally caught in the filaments of the lotus pollen.

By the touch of even a mere particle of dust raised by the wind from the reeds on your banks, this person’s sins are instantly destroyed; and through your grace, O purifier of the world, he holds even the station of Indra in contempt.

We bow at your feet, which forcibly serve as the dwelling for the mass of matted hair of the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva), whose shimmering footstool is illuminated by the radiance of the reflections of various kinds of countless jewel-rays from the crowns of millions of gods prostrating during the three junctions of the day.
Whoever should recite this beautiful octet concerning the daughter of Jahnu, composed by Kālidāsa at all three times of day,
shall never fail to attain the youthful state of Lord Keśava, whose station is sung of even by Indra and the other gods.
Thus ends the Gaṅgāṣṭaka Stotra composed by the illustrious Kālidāsa.
